Sell
sel
v.t. (rendering Hebrew makar, Greek pōleō)
From Saxon syllan, to give, deliver, or sell. Hebrew makar is to sell, and is used with terrible force of God selling a disobedient people into the hand of their enemies — a transfer of possession that is also a judgment.

Biblical Definition

Selling in Scripture exposes what a man values, because a sale reveals the seller's estimate of what he parted with. Esau's bargain is the standing example: “And Jacob said, Sell me this day thy birthright” (Genesis 25:31) — and the epistle to the Hebrews calls him a profane person who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright, which is what every sale of the eternal for the immediate amounts to. The rich young ruler is met at exactly the point where his estimate lay: “If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven” (Matthew 19:21) — a command that exposed a god, and the man went away sorrowful. In the parable the merchant sells with joy, not grief: “when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matthew 13:46). And Ananias sold honestly and lied about the price: “a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession” (Acts 5:1) — the sin was not in selling or in keeping back part, as Peter says plainly, but in the pretence. Selling is therefore a moral disclosure. What a man will part with, what he will not, and what he will lie about, together make a fair account of his heart.

Webster 1828 Definition

To transfer property to another for an equivalent in money; to part with for a price. In Scripture, Esau selling his birthright, the ruler commanded to sell what he had, the merchant who sold all for one pearl, and Ananias who sold a possession and lied about the price.

expand to see more

SELL, v.t. 1. To transfer property, or the exclusive right of possession, to another for an equivalent in money.

2. To make a matter of bargain and sale; to accept a price or reward for; as, to sell one's honour.

3. To betray for a consideration; as, Judas sold his Master.

4. From Saxon syllan, to deliver, to give over; Hebrew makar, to sell.

5. In Scripture, sell me this day thy birthright, Gen. 25; sold all that he had, and bought it, Matt. 13.

Key Scripture

Genesis 25:31 — "And Jacob said, Sell me this day thy birthright."

Matthew 19:21 — "Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me."

Matthew 13:46 — "Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it."

Acts 5:1 — "But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession,"

Modern Corruption

The command to the rich young ruler is universalised into a rule that possessions are sinful, or else neutralised entirely so that it asks nothing of anyone; and generosity is performed for reputation, which is the sin Ananias died for.

expand to see more

Two opposite mishandlings of Matthew 19:21 are common. Liberation theology and its evangelical imitators universalise it: property is inherently oppressive, and the gospel is a programme of redistribution, so that a man's standing before God is measured by his economics. Scripture forbids the generalisation — Abraham, Job, Lydia, and Philemon were all people of means, believers are commanded to provide for their own houses, and the eighth commandment presupposes lawful property. The opposite evasion is more comfortable and just as false: because the command was addressed to one man, it is treated as asking nothing of anyone now. But the Lord aimed at the ruler's god, and He still does. The question the passage puts is not whether every Christian must liquidate but what a man would refuse Christ if He asked for it — and most men know the answer before they finish the sentence.

Ananias is the other warning, and Peter's words remove every excuse from it: whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? The property was his, the sale was voluntary, and the amount given was entirely at his discretion. What killed him was the performance — the appearance of a total gift where a partial one had been made, generosity staged for the admiration of the church. That sin is not extinct; it has merely acquired better instruments, since giving can now be publicised at scale. The principle to recover is our Lord's own in Matthew 6: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth. Real generosity is answerable to God, who sees in secret, and needs no witnesses at all.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew makar, to sell, and figuratively to deliver over in judgment; mimkar, a sale or thing sold; Greek pōleō, to sell, and pipraskoo, to sell, especially into slavery.

expand to see more

Hebrew makar (H4376) — to sell; used of Joseph sold by his brethren and of Israel sold into the hand of her enemies (Judges 2:14).

Hebrew mimkar (H4465) — a sale, or the thing sold; governed in Israel by the jubilee laws of Leviticus 25.

Greek pōleō (G4453) — to sell; the verb of the merchant who sold all for the pearl (Matthew 13:46).

Greek pipraskoo (G4097) — to sell, often into bondage; “sold under sin” (Romans 7:14).

Greek bēbēlos (G952) — profane, unhallowed; the epithet given Esau for selling his birthright (Hebrews 12:16).

Usage

"Of the eternal traded for the immediate: Sell me this day thy birthright (Genesis 25:31)."

"Of a command that exposed an idol: go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor (Matthew 19:21)."

"Of joyful, total exchange: went and sold all that he had, and bought it (Matthew 13:46)."
